title: Foundational Document on the Agricultural College

sections.title: Definition
sections.body: The Agricultural College is a peer body of practitioners skilled in the cultivation of plants, stewardship of land, and raising of livestock. Its purpose is to maintain standards of agricultural practice, transmit knowledge to new practitioners, supply qualified members for sortition to agricultural oversight committees, and exercise governance authority over the Agricultural Service's functions as delegated by the General Assembly.
sections.rationale: Food security and land stewardship are fundamental to community survival. The College ensures that the community maintains genuine competence in these essential disciplines.

sections.title: Domain
sections.body: The College's domain includes: crop cultivation (field crops, vegetables, orchards, herbs), soil management (composting, amendments, fertility, conservation), water management (irrigation, drainage, conservation), livestock husbandry (if practiced), integrated pest management, seed saving and plant propagation, seasonal planning and crop rotation, and land stewardship practices. The domain may expand as the College develops capacity in additional agricultural disciplines.
sections.rationale: Clear domain definition prevents scope creep while allowing organic growth as practitioners develop new knowledge and adapt to local conditions.

sections.title: Relationship to Services
sections.body: Members of the Agricultural College may work in the Agricultural Service, Food Service's kitchen gardens, or any other Service requiring agricultural skills. College membership is not required for Service employment. College membership places a practitioner in the qualified sortition pool for governance functions requiring agricultural expertise.
sections.rationale: Separating civic credentials from employment prevents the College from becoming a closed shop while maintaining its governance function.

sections.title: Eligibility
sections.body: Membership is open to any Society member who demonstrates competence in one or more agricultural disciplines within the College's domain. Competence may be demonstrated through: production records and harvest documentation, land management outcomes assessed by existing members, completion of apprenticeship under a College member, supervised growing seasons, or documented professional experience.
sections.rationale: Multiple pathways to membership recognize that agricultural skills can be developed through formal training, apprenticeship, family tradition, or independent practice.

sections.title: Peer Assessment
sections.body: Existing College members assess applicants' agricultural knowledge and practice, evaluating their understanding of soil health, crop requirements, pest management, and sustainable land use. Assessment focuses on demonstrated competence in growing healthy crops, maintaining soil fertility, and working with natural systems rather than maximizing yield or efficiency.
sections.rationale: Peers are best positioned to recognize genuine agricultural competence. Emphasis on soil health and sustainability ensures the College credentials practitioners who build long-term productive capacity.

sections.title: Ecological Awareness
sections.body: All members must demonstrate understanding of ecological relationships: soil biology, nutrient cycles, beneficial insects, water cycles, and the impact of agricultural practices on surrounding ecosystems. The College prioritizes regenerative practices that build soil health and support biodiversity.
sections.rationale: Agriculture that degrades soil and ecosystems undermines the community's long-term food security. The College has a duty to credential practitioners who understand their role as stewards rather than extractors.

sections.title: Specialization
sections.body: Members need not be competent in all agricultural disciplines to join the College. A market gardener, an orchardist, and a grain farmer bring different skills. All are members. When the Assembly draws from the College for a committee requiring specific agricultural expertise, the draw may be limited to members credentialed in the relevant discipline.
sections.rationale: Recognizing specialization within a broad college allows the community to develop deep expertise in specific crops and methods while maintaining a unified agricultural peer body.

sections.title: Apprenticeship and Knowledge Transmission
sections.body: The College encourages members to take apprentices and transmit their skills to new practitioners. Successful completion of apprenticeship under a College member is a recognized path to membership. The College may establish apprenticeship standards but shall not make formal apprenticeship the only path to membership.
sections.rationale: Apprenticeship preserves place-based agricultural knowledge across generations while preventing gatekeeping through excessive formalization. Farm knowledge is often best transmitted through direct mentorship.

sections.title: Standards of Practice
sections.body: The College maintains written standards of sustainable agricultural practice for each discipline within its domain. Standards shall be accessible to all members and shall be revised as the community develops site-specific knowledge. Standards serve as teaching tools and quality benchmarks, not as rigid prescriptions.
sections.rationale: Documented standards prevent knowledge loss and provide clear guidance for new practitioners while allowing experienced members to exercise judgment based on local conditions.

sections.title: Seed and Variety Knowledge
sections.body: The College maintains institutional knowledge about crop varieties suited to local conditions, seed saving practices, plant propagation techniques, and varietal characteristics. This knowledge shall be documented and made available to all practitioners. The College may maintain a seed library for the community.
sections.rationale: Varietal knowledge adapted to local soil and climate is irreplaceable. Communities that lose their seeds and seed knowledge lose agricultural resilience. The College prevents this loss by maintaining institutional memory.

sections.title: Seasonal Planning and Records
sections.body: The College encourages members to maintain planting records, harvest logs, and seasonal observations. These records build collective understanding of local growing conditions, successful crop rotations, and climate patterns over time. Aggregated records help the community adapt to changing conditions.
sections.rationale: Agricultural knowledge is built through observation across many growing seasons. Individual records become community wisdom when shared.

sections.title: Soil Knowledge
sections.body: The College holds institutional knowledge about local soil types, amendment practices, composting methods, cover cropping, and long-term soil building. This knowledge shall be documented and shared with all land stewards in the community. Soil health is the foundation of food security.
sections.rationale: Soil degradation can occur within a generation but restoration takes decades. The College serves the community by maintaining and transmitting knowledge of regenerative soil practices.

sections.title: Knowledge Sharing
sections.body: College members shall actively share knowledge with apprentices, interested community members, and each other. The College may organize field days, seed swaps, seasonal workshops, and collaborative experiments. Agricultural knowledge is a community resource, not private property.
sections.rationale: Mutual aid societies thrive on knowledge sharing. Hoarding expertise undermines the College's purpose and the community's food security.

sections.title: Experimentation and Adaptation
sections.body: The College encourages members to trial new crops, test growing methods, observe results, and share findings. Experimentation shall be documented and results shared rather than kept as individual trade secrets. Climate change and local conditions require ongoing adaptation.
sections.rationale: Small communities need practitioners who can experiment and adapt to changing conditions. Encouraging experimentation while requiring documentation builds collective resilience.

sections.title: Agricultural Service Oversight
sections.body: When the General Assembly establishes a committee to oversee the Agricultural Service, it shall draw members from the Agricultural College. The College does not govern the Agricultural Service directly—that authority comes from the Assembly's delegation to the drawn committee.
sections.rationale: Qualified sortition ensures that people with actual agricultural expertise oversee agricultural work, while maintaining democratic legitimacy through random selection from a credentialed pool.

sections.title: Land Use Guidance
sections.body: When drawn committee members participate in decisions about agricultural land use, crop planning, or soil management practices, they bring the College's collective knowledge to bear on governance questions. They serve as representatives of agricultural practice, not as representatives of the College as an organization.
sections.rationale: Sortition combines technical expertise with random selection to prevent capture while ensuring informed decision-making.

sections.title: Food Security Planning
sections.body: College members drawn to governance roles may participate in community food security planning, evaluating crop diversity, storage capacity, preservation methods, and seasonal food availability. Their technical knowledge serves the community's long-term resilience.
sections.rationale: Food security requires both production capacity and systems thinking. Practitioners understand what can realistically be grown, stored, and preserved in local conditions.

sections.title: No Monopoly on Governance
sections.body: The College supplies credentialed practitioners for qualified sortition but does not claim monopoly authority over agricultural decisions. The General Assembly retains ultimate authority over agricultural policy. The College's role is to ensure that when the Assembly seeks agricultural expertise, such expertise is genuinely available.
sections.rationale: Preventing guild capture requires that ultimate authority remain with the democratic body while still utilizing practitioner knowledge through sortition.

sections.title: Annual Report
sections.body: The College shall submit an annual report to the General Assembly documenting: current membership count, new members admitted, knowledge-sharing activities conducted, standards updated or established, and any concerns about community agricultural capacity or soil health. The report is descriptive, not prescriptive.
sections.rationale: Transparency ensures the Assembly can assess whether the College is fulfilling its knowledge-transmission function and maintaining genuine standards.

sections.title: Membership Records
sections.body: The College shall maintain clear records of members and their credentialed specializations, making this information available to the Assembly for sortition purposes. Membership criteria and assessment processes shall be documented and publicly accessible.
sections.rationale: Sortition requires clear knowledge of who is in the pool and what expertise they bring. Transparency in membership prevents favoritism and maintains legitimacy.

sections.title: Standards Availability
sections.body: All College standards, knowledge documents, and educational materials shall be publicly available to the community. The College does not hoard knowledge behind membership walls.
sections.rationale: The College serves the community by developing and maintaining agricultural knowledge. That knowledge must be accessible to all, whether or not they seek College membership.

sections.title: Dissolution Clause
sections.body: If the College fails to maintain genuine standards, ceases knowledge-sharing activities, or becomes a vehicle for rent-seeking rather than knowledge transmission, the General Assembly may dissolve it by supermajority vote. Dissolution returns all College functions and records to the Assembly. Members retain their individual agricultural knowledge and practice rights.
sections.rationale: Colleges exist to serve community needs, not to entrench privilege. The dissolution clause ensures accountability and prevents institutional decay.
